Analyze this product review:

It took me a long time to find a good new smart watch. My main issue was BATTERY. A Fitbit needs to be charged every day! And it never charged enough during my shower to last for the next day. I loved my Fitbit otherwise, but stopped using it because I refuse to have to think about charging a watch every day.
Right now and after over a month of use with all my options and apps set, my Garmin can last 10 days!!! And I receive my texts and calls, morning alarms, it's connected in Bluetooth to my phone nonstop, so it vibrates a lot.
BATTERY 100/10 AMAZING
Then the functions of course. I'm a geek and love gadgets so I had a lot of fun looking through faces and apps and shortcuts and all. It can be daunting for non-geeks. In the end I settled for a lot of the Garmin apps because they work great! I really wanted a Torchlight option, with different colors and a SOS option because I'm into surviving any situation. I got the Magic Rescue app, which I do not like very much but it lets you save 3 emergency phone numbers for you or for rescuers, in case you lose your phone. My favorite is Brighty. It has different brightness and colors and a SOS option that can run until the battery dies, exactly what I wanted. I set up a button shortcut for it so I have a Torchlight handy on my wrist.
There's a lot to say about that watch. The reviews saying it takes too long to launch an activity must be technologically inept, as you just need to swipe left? Or touch the upper button? (You can change the function of these buttons like I did but from the get-go, activities are RIGHT THERE).
Issues:
- smart alarm is not great. I had an app on my phone 10 years ago that detected the end of my sleep cycle accurately and woke me up then. The watch has been pretty random, and also vibrates once and that's it? Not happy with that function.
- bluetooth disconnects very often. It's a pain as I use my watch at work, where I cannot check my phone, so not receiving texts because of a Bluetooth issue is really annoying. It's an easy fix but still.
- some Garmin apps measure your body temperature, but the watch does not have that option. It's ok, just a little bit sad about that parameter not being available on my brand new expensive watch.
- I got the white bracelet and it's already dirty. It's a bit annoying, as I expect high quality. It's ok.
- does not detect and start an activity automatically. My Fitbit would detect that I was walking or swimming (even though it thought I was swimming when I was folding laundry). My Garmin just does not start, even though I saw that setting, and told it to start the activity 10 minutes after it was detected. It also does not stop it either. Please make an update as I do not always remember to start the activity before I walk (I walk a lot and all day) or swim (I just forget). Maybe I'll review the options and settings again, because I really want this to happen.
When you do start a hike, the watch makes a neat little map, and will help you find your way back to the starting point if you get lost (yay survival!)
Cool things I didn't know I needed:
- controlling my Spotify and Google maps on my watch! Seeing pictures I am sent by text, on my watch! This is so damn cool. I am not an Apple person besides the iPad so I feel fancy at a lower price.
- again: When you do start a hike, the watch makes a neat little map, and will help you find your way back to the starting point if you get lost (yay survival!)
I love my new watch! I hope it lasts for a couple of years.

Analyze this product review:

After being a Fitbit loyalist for a number of years, I made the switch to Garmin after the recent hostile Google takeover of the Fitbit platform. I went with the Vivoactive 6 because I wanted to have a decent number of functions without being overcomplicated. I was kind of “meh” about it at first, but after playing with settings and finding my groove, I’m officially in love.
First off, like most Garmin models, it’s advertised as having “up to” 11 days of battery life. I imagine this would only be achievable if you were using it solely as a watch and had most/all tracking settings turned off. When I first got it, I left Move IQ turned on—this is the setting that auto-detects activity like walks and runs when you’ve been moving for at least 10 minutes (or however long you specify). I got about 6 days of battery out of that first charge, which is what I was getting on my Fitbit, so I considered this acceptable.
But I decided to experiment and try some new settings after the second charge. I disabled Move IQ, which means I now have to manually start and stop any activities when I’m doing them. I like that you can create a quick access menu of your most common activities. This really isn’t so bad—the trick is just remembering to do it 😅. Sometimes I’ll go for a walk and forget to start it. The watch still tracks the steps and reads the elevated heart rate, but it just won’t say “YES HELLO YOU WENT FOR A WALK” afterward. Which is kinda silly, but oh well. You know you did it. I got 9 days of battery life this time and still had 10% left when I charged it, so I think I’ll keep using it like this.
The sleep tracking has seemed accurate so far; Fitbit used to do a good job too until the Google Health transition. Heart rate has seemed more accurate as well; there were times when Fitbit would say I was only at 80 bpm when I could check manually and tell it was at least 120.
There are so many things you can customize, whether it’s the color and layout of the watch face or which metrics are displayed on the watch, in the app, or not displayed/tracked at all. I love a good aesthetic.
So anyway. I’m very pleased so far. My tricks for conserving battery life are:
- keep Move IQ turned off and manually track activities
- disable Always On Display during activity
- block notifications from any unnecessary apps (by default you’ll get ALL notifications from your phone—I set mine to only get texts, calls, Messenger, Teams, and calendar reminders)
- set a Do Not Disturb timeframe overnight

Analyze this product review:

I have been using fitness trackers/smart watches from different vendors.
I decided to switch because my last one was occasionally over-estimating my heart rate and sleep time.
I pick Garmin because reviews are saying it is very good at tracking, even though lower end models including this one have Elevate Gen4 sensor, not gen5. And also, it has a good battery life and lightweight.
This is my first Garmin.
So what do I like about it:
- it is extremely comfortable and lightweight indeed - both watch and braselet
- tracking is very adequate except it sometimes over-estimate heart rate - see below
- you do not need subscription to use it or see the history (but see below)
- looks beautiful and stylish
- the watch face I have found has day and night mode and in night mode it is very dim and drawn with thin lines - that is awesome!
- buttons and navigation are nice
So why only 4 starts?
- charging cable is plug-in, not magnetic, and usb-c to usb-c - make sure you have a charger for it!
- when it arrives, it needs software update. Do not even try software update from the phone - it downloads software for hours but does not update the watch in the end. Run updates from the watch. You might need multiple iterations.
- faces it comes with are cheesy. Weirdly, you will need to install an additional phone app to install faces. Most of them are paid, but you can get some nice free ones. Watch out - some "free" faces will ask for money after a week of use.
- there is  a software bug in the app - you cannot add widgets like sleep to the main "at a glance" - only remove. You can still combine sleep from "in focus" with steps and heart rate from "in glance" but... This barely works. I mean, you can still find everything, but do you want to dig through the app every time you start it? "At a glance" is what we need, but config is broken.
- the bracelet is too soft and it takes some effort to put the watch on a hand. First time I spent half a minute. Yes, it is really that tricky. Yet, you might not want to replace it because it is so soft and comfy once you put it on a hand!
- the display is small. You might think it is as large as the watch face, but no, there are ridiculously wide dark borders around it. You can see it when you scroll the watch. The screen is still usable, but larger screen would be nice.
After a month of use:
Heart rate measurement is somewhat better than in 4x cheaper model from a different vendor, but not always accurate. Sleep monitoring is somewhat worse - there are both "false positives" and "false negatives" occasionally.
As for steps counting - depends what do you need. If you need coarse counting - it can do it. If you need to walk 300 steps and do something and repeat - this overpriced toy absolutely cannot do it. For some reason, the steps number on the watch screen is updated every 70 steps or so, not in real time. So it absolutely cannot do some basic fitness tracker tasks. It still can show you time and heart rate and messages and can annoy you with some daily reports, so it is not completely useless. Much cheaper trackers from different vendors can show you steps in real time. But if accurate real-time steps counting is not needed - it is Ok tracker (though, very overpriced for the functionality it offers).
I also added my workouts through the web site and tried to use the Vivoactive for workout. I gave up on the watch interface (no way to stop exercise without deleting, not stopping when it should, etc - very confusing). It also does not track exercises nearly as accurately as Garmin video claims, even for hands - very frustrating.
I am still happy with watch quality, battery life, and how comfortable it is to wear.
Update: it does not track daytime nap. Basic fitness trackers from the other brands do.
Based on the functionality this smartwatch offers, fair price should be somewhere below $50.

Dell 24 Plus Monitor - S2425HSM
CONS
There is no option to hook up a USB-C or thunderbolt cable on this monitor. Thus you can not charge your laptop by plugging it into the monitor.
This monitor is designed so that you plug an HDMI cable into your laptop and then into the monitor. HDMI cables are bulky and don’t bend as easily as a USB-C or Thunderbolt cable. HDMI cables do not charge your laptop. USB-C or Thunderbolt cables are more bendy and charge your laptop directly from your monitor.
You cannot have your MacBook in clamshell mode (laptop closed) without having your laptop charging cable plugged in. Thus instead of one USB-C or Thunderbolt cable you have the bulky HDMI and your laptops power cord. When I had all the cables hooked up it felt messy and it was all sort of awkwardly mashed into the desk riser I built.
The text resolution of this monitor was pretty pixilated. Downloading Better Display and creating a virtual screen helped a bit.

144Hz refresh rate

It’s so odd but I completely fell in love with this monitor despite the fact that it really didn’t meet any of my core needs. I loved the color, the sleek design and the ease of the mini joystick on the monitor itself. I barely was able to return this monitor because I was weirdly attached to it. I’d say this is perfect for a high school or college student. - 100Hz refresh keeps motion blur and lag down, which is plenty for the gaming I do

- Built-in speakers mean no extra clutter on the desk for casual video calls and content
- Extra HDMI and connectivity ports make it easy to plug devices straight in

- At 32 inches, FHD resolution means pixel density is on the modest side — fine for gaming and media, but text isn't razor-sharp if I sit very close
- The built-in speakers are serviceable, not impressive; I still reach for headphones for music

As someone who reads reviews, even for the smallest of purchases, I had the WORST time finding one from someone who knew what they were getting when they bought the Lily 2. So, I'm writing this on the understanding that no one will likely ever see it, since this watch has been out for more than a year.
Having been a Galaxy watch owner since the 4 came out, I upgraded to the 7 this year, simply because it's cheaper to keep upgrading than it is to buy new. While these watches work well and have a lot of features, I'd started to wonder if I even needed one anymore. I've never used the majority of the features offered and find myself only really wanting the practical ones, like notifications, "find my phone," timers, answering calls from my watch when my earbuds are in and my phone is in another room, and the actual clock. I also liked some of the health features like heart rate and fitness tracking. All the other stuff had just become noise that had overwhelmed me to the point that I wasn't even using the things I did like. In addition, I find traditional smartwatches ugly and clunky, no matter how pretty the band, because I have a slender wrist and they're all huge. So, when I received a full refund for my Galaxy Watch 7, after it malfunctioned, I decided to try something else. Enter the Lily 2.
I scoured the internet for reviews on this watch, because while simpler, it's actually not cheaper than the alternatives and I was unfamiliar with Garmin. Every review I read included negatives for things like lacking GPS, not offering a lot of customization, and battery life. Many recommended larger and more complicated Garmin watches instead. The thing is, I don't WANT these features, ESPECIALLY when the trade-off is a larger watch. Yes, the Lily 2 Active has GPS and a longer battery life, but I don't go anywhere without my phone and my Galaxy Watch had to be charged nightly. GPS is not a benefit to me, nor is longer than a 5 day battery if it makes the watch only 2mm smaller than my Galaxy Watch. Other recommendations were actually even BIGGER. At 35mm, this watch is so small, it looks closer to actual watch size on my wrist. The lack of customization is what makes it so pretty. This machine took a hot minute to get set up and working, but once I got it all sorted out, it did a great job of making espresso with ease.
I have to mention that I didn't realize that there is a red rubber bit on the bottom of the water bin that needed removing, so I had an issue with getting water into the machine initially. Once I realized my mistake and removed the red rubber piece, the machine worked great.
There is a method to getting the coffee grinder top clicked into the machine. Two nubs need to be lined up in order to get it to sit before twisting and locking it in place. I mention this because the instructions don't, and it took about 10 minutes of both of us fiddling with it before we figured it out and got it locked into place.
The beans grind beautifully. I put it on 25, which is a fine grind, and it did a beautiful job of finely grinding the coffee. I like this feature a lot because I prefer to brew a double shot, and now the machine is set to do that every morning.
The first time I pulled two shots, it didn't get up to the correct bar pressure, and the coffee dribbled out of the spout. So I tried again, and it came out better and was close to the optimal bar pressure, but still not perfect. On my third try, it hit the perfect bar pressure and the coffee came out in a nice stream with a good head on top. So it took a bit for the machine to kick in, but once it did, it worked quickly and made excellent espresso.
The milk frother worked perfectly on my first try. It did a nice job of steaming and bubbling the half and half that I used.
Now for the important part: the taste. The espresso is excellent! The color is dark, and the flavor is strong and rich. I expected it from this machine because I have the small, inexpensive version that sells for around $125.00, and we use that more often than a $600 espresso machine that we also have at the other house. That machine is currently in our other house, and we didn't have an espresso machine here in our summer home. Anyway, this machine didn't disappoint. It makes an excellent cappuccino! I make mine with three shots of espresso, and this is perfect in the morning.
This machine, being offered at $399.99, is an excellent value for a machine with so many features. It truly makes an excellent espresso, and once it's set up, it's easy and quick to operate. This is a must for me because I don't function well before coffee! The machine is beautiful, and it's good quality. It stacks up nicely when compared to the big-name, expensive machines. I'm really happy with the quality and ease of use, and I recommend this espresso maker and the brand for excellent espressos.

The Razer Huntsman V3 Pro TKL 8KHz is an easy 5-star keyboard for me because of the performance and the level of control it gives you. The biggest highlight is the adjustable actuation: being able to set the exact actuation point (in millimeters) completely changes how the keyboard feels. On the performance side, the 8KHz polling rate adds to that “instant” feel. It’s not magic, but compared to standard keyboards it does feel more direct and consistent, especially in competitive games where you want inputs to be as fast and repeatable as possible.
Customization is another major win. You can create profiles per game and fine-tune different keys differently—for example, setting WASD to a shorter actuation while keeping other keys at a more normal setting. That kind of flexibility makes the keyboard feel tailored instead of one-size-fits-all.
Even as a TKL, it’s the ideal format for me: more desk space for mouse movement, better posture, and you still keep everything you actually need for gaming. Build quality is also very good—the keyboard feels solid, well-made, and premium overall. Finally, the design/style I chose (the Niko Edition) looks absolutely beautiful in person and makes the whole setup look even better.

First, I had refused for years to get a Keurig, as I did not feel the quality and richness of a good strong cup of coffee was possible. But I finally got tired of trying other methods of brewing, from using a regular single cup espresso maker, moka pot, pour over, French press... I finally opted for the ease of a Keurig mini-plus. Coffee was ...eh... I switched coffee brands, to what I feel has to be the best commercial brand. And the coffee was EXcellenT! About a year later, despite regular cleaning cycles, the thing just stopped working. I tried to take it apart, watched some youtube videos which just solidified the fact that the company made these non-serviceable. P.O.'d at this obvious tactic to sell more, I waited a few weeks, but went and got another one. Same deal a year later. Another one. This last one gave me signs before ending it's own life. I would have to run several cycles where nothing would come out... till finally something... drip... by drip... several hours later, the thing would start running again, only to stop again the next day or two. Finally, it just died.
So I REFUSED to get another. These things are ridiculous, right? So I got a new French press. Coffee is great!! But... omg... what a pain cleaning that thing every.... single... time... I mean, really, it's no big deal. But, it CAn be. So I saw this thing on sale, I thought, well, it's HAlf the price of the other ones... and I def want something different this time. Cut to now....
This thing has SEVERAL issues that I don't like. First of all, it is a thinner cheaper plastic, and has a cheap looking shine to it. Ok, I'm over it. The plastic... I mean, can't they make these things with glass reservoirs.... the plastic reservoir has screws on the inside of it. I don't care if they say it is food safe... Plastic is also considered food safe... but that doesn't mean it is.. those are just bureaucratic rhetoric lies. But I digress,...So this coffee maker has an adjustment for high altitude... is THAT what ruined my previous Keurigs? High altitude? Hmmm. Ok, so maybe that's a plus. It also has different sizes that you can choose -8,10, & 12 oz. With the mini-plus, you choose the size by the amount of water you pour in. That means that this one measures what it sucks in. Hmmm. The mini-plus had the controls on the top. Easy peasy. This one has the controls on the side. It also doesn't have rubber feet on the bottom. So when you try to push the buttons, the thing slides away from you. Impossible to push any buttons with one hand, you have to use two. Even with rubber feet, you have to use two hands. I'm not a paraplegic, but it's rather stupid to have to hold the thing to press a button or two, or three. Which is what you have to do. It's just really awkward because you really have to hold it in the back to keep it from moving when you press the button in front. And you have to do that without touching the reservoir, which will pop out if you tried that.
But let's get to the coffee. So with the mini-plus, the first liquid out of the machine, was dark coffee. As it was finishing, the coffee would be a little more clear, but not pure water. With this machine, for the first few seconds, it is spewing out crystal clear WATER. I don't even know how that is possible. But this, it does. It also claims to be faster than the mini-cup. I hestitate to say "brews faster", because it doesn't brew, Keurigs simply spew water into and through the k-cup, it's a pressurized system, not a true brewing system. And it definitely IS faster. And that's a problem, as evidenced by the watery coffee that it spews out. Sure enough, the "coffee" tastes like water. This is the 8 oz brew, mind you, with the machine set to "strong". I first tried the 12oz, and ended up pouring it down the sink. The 8 oz wasn't much better. My next step is to switch out cups while it's pouring out the water at the beginning of the cycle and see if I can get a stronger "brew".
All in all, it's convenient enough. But it will sit on my counter, mostly unused, for when I have those really lazy, sleepy, or sick days, when all I want to do is pop in a capsule, and deal with the rest of it... Very disappointed. Perhaps if you live in a low altitude area, the mini-plus would work for you. I really do recommend that one above this.
